name: Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies

clinicalPearls: This chapter covers the uncommon hematologic neoplasms, each individually accounting for under 1% of hematologic malignancies; the rare lymphoid tumors are all mature B-cell, T-cell, or NK-cell neoplasms (Harrison 22e p.871).

Splenic marginal zone lymphoma cells express surface immunoglobulin and CD20 but are negative for CD5, CD10, CD43, and CD103; absence of CD5 separates it from CLL and absence of CD103 separates it from hairy cell leukemia, and circulating cells are villous lymphocytes (Harrison 22e p.872).

Hairy cell leukemia is a frequent cause of a 'dry tap' on marrow aspiration because of increased reticulin fibers; it shows profound monocytopenia (predisposing to atypical mycobacterial infection), strong CD22/CD25/CD103 expression, tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase positivity, and the activating BRAF V600E mutation in most cases (Harrison 22e p.872-873).

Mediastinal (thymic) large B-cell lymphoma typically remains confined to the mediastinum, affects women more than men (ratio about 1:2-3) at a median age of 35-40 years, is CD20 positive and CD45 positive (unlike classical Hodgkin's), and may lack surface immunoglobulin and HLA class I/II expression (Harrison 22e p.873).

Primary effusion lymphoma presents with effusions usually without a tumor mass, is caused by HHV-8/KSHV (often EBV co-infected), occurs mainly in immunodeficiency such as AIDS, and follows a rapidly fatal course (Harrison 22e p.873).

T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia is aggressive with very high WBC counts often exceeding 100,000/uL, hepatosplenomegaly, and adenopathy; chromosome 14 inversion between q11 and q32 occurs in about 80% of patients (Harrison 22e p.874).

T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia is dominated by severe neutropenia and is frequently associated with systemic autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis; pure red cell aplasia occurs in 15-20% and the course is generally indolent (Harrison 22e p.874).

Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, is an EBV-related angiocentric/angiodestructive CD56-positive lesion prevalent in Asia, Mexico, and Central/South America; historic names include lethal midline granuloma and polymorphic reticulosis (Harrison 22e p.874).

Enteropathy-type T-cell lymphoma is a rare complication of longstanding celiac disease, usually arising in jejunum or ileum, with most patients carrying the celiac-associated HLA DQA1*0501 or DQB1*0201 genotype (Harrison 22e p.874).

Chronic neutrophilic leukemia is a clonal proliferation of mature neutrophils molecularly defined by activating CSF3R mutations (most commonly the membrane-proximal T618I, found in about 90% of cases); diagnosis requires excluding reactive neutrophilia and other myeloid neoplasms (Harrison 22e p.875-876).

Systemic mastocytosis diagnosis rests on a major criterion (multifocal aggregates of >=15 mast cells) or three minor criteria including >25% atypical mast cells, aberrant mast cell expression of CD25/CD2/CD30, KIT D816V or other activating KIT mutation, and serum tryptase >20 ng/mL (Harrison 22e p.881).

Transient myeloproliferative disorder occurs in about 10% of infants with Down syndrome, carries somatic GATA1 mutations, and either regresses spontaneously (about 75%) or progresses to acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (about 25%) (Harrison 22e p.879).
harrison.pathophysiology: These entities are individually rare clonal neoplasms of the lymphoid or myeloid lineages. Rare lymphoid tumors are mature B-cell, T-cell, or NK-cell neoplasms; several B-cell variants of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma have distinctive biology, such as intravascular large B-cell lymphoma (confined to vessel lumens, postulated to reflect defective adhesion molecule and homing function with absent beta-1 integrin and ICAM-1), primary effusion lymphoma (HHV-8/KSHV-driven, frequently EBV co-infected), and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (an angiodestructive EBV-infected monoclonal B-cell proliferation outnumbered by reactive T cells). Many T/NK entities are EBV-associated and angiocentric. On the myeloid side, distinct molecular drivers define the entities: activating CSF3R mutations in chronic neutrophilic leukemia, GM-CSF hypersensitivity from dysregulated RAS/MAPK signaling (mutually exclusive RAS, PTPN11, NF1 mutations) in juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia, somatic GATA1 mutations in transient myeloproliferative disorder of Down syndrome, and constitutively active tyrosine kinase gene fusions (involving PDGFRA such as FIP1L1-PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, ABL1, JAK2, FLT3) in eosinophilic myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms. Mastocytosis reflects neoplastic mast cell proliferation typically driven by KIT D816V. Dendritic/histiocytic neoplasms arise from antigen-presenting or antigen-processing cell lineages; Langerhans cell histiocytosis cells are S100+/CD1a+ with Birbeck granules and about 55% carry BRAF V600E.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (distinguished from splenic marginal zone lymphoma by CD5 positivity)
Mantle cell lymphoma (overlaps with B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia via CD5 and t(11;14))
Nodular sclerosing Hodgkin's disease (versus mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma; the latter is CD45 positive, lacks lacunar Reed-Sternberg variants)
Anaplastic large T-cell lymphoma with t(2;5) (versus primary cutaneous CD30+ T-cell lymphoma, which lacks t(2;5))
Chronic myeloid leukemia, BCR::ABL1 positive (versus atypical CML and chronic neutrophilic leukemia)
infectionMimics: Reactive neutrophilia from infection or inflammation (mimics chronic neutrophilic leukemia)
Reactive monocytosis from tuberculosis, fungal infection, subacute bacterial endocarditis, viral or protozoal infection (mimics chronic myelomonocytic leukemia)
Hypereosinophilia from tissue-invasive helminths and other parasitic infection (mimics primary/clonal eosinophilic disorders)
nonInfectiousMimics: Plasma cell neoplasms and metastatic solid tumors producing secondary neutrophilia (mimic chronic neutrophilic leukemia)
Connective tissue disease, sarcoidosis, lipid storage disorders, postsplenectomy state, and marrow regeneration after chemotherapy (mimic CMML monocytosis)
Allergic/vasculitic disease and drug reactions (mimic primary hypereosinophilia)
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (raises serum tryptase, confounding mastocytosis criteria)
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood smear and bone marrow morphology with immunophenotyping/flow cytometry for lineage markers
Cytogenetics and molecular testing: CSF3R (CNL), KIT D816V (mastocytosis), GATA1 (transient myeloproliferative disorder), SETBP1, RAS-pathway mutations (JMML)
FISH or RT-PCR screening for PDGFRA and PDGFRB rearrangements in hypereosinophilia
Serum tryptase (mast cell disease; elevation also prompts FIP1L1-PDGFRA testing) and soluble CD25 as a hairy cell leukemia activity marker
T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies and T-cell immunophenotyping in hypereosinophilia to detect lymphocytic-variant disease
Echocardiogram and serum troponin to screen for cardiac involvement in hypereosinophilic syndrome (apical thrombus, endocardial thickening, valve abnormality)
Electron microscopy/immunostaining for Birbeck granules, CD1a, S100, and langerin in Langerhans cell histiocytosis
redFlags: Aggressive NK cell leukemia presenting with fever, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, hemophagocytosis, coagulopathy, or multiorgan failure
Intravascular large B-cell lymphoma with small-vessel occlusion, neurologic symptoms, and thrombus formation, often diagnosed only late or at autopsy
Hemophagocytic syndrome complicating extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma or subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma (can drive a fulminant downhill course)
Cardiac involvement in hypereosinophilic syndrome (cardiomyopathy, ventricular apical thrombus, elevated troponin)

Mast cell organopathy C findings: cytopenias, hepatomegaly with portal hypertension/ascites, splenomegaly with hypersplenism, GI infiltration with malabsorption and weight loss, large osteolytic lesions with pathologic fractures
True mast cell leukemia, regarded as an oncologic emergency requiring expedited diagnosis
Bowel perforation from tumor response in treated enteropathy-type T-cell lymphoma
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes vary widely by entity. Indolent disorders include splenic marginal zone lymphoma (median survival over 10 years), T-cell large granular lymphocytic leukemia, and primary cutaneous CD30+ T-cell lymphoma (5-year survival over 90%). Aggressive entities carry poor outcomes: T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (median survival about 12 months), enteropathy-type T-cell lymphoma (median 7-11 months), hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma (median about 2 years), primary effusion lymphoma (death typically within 6 months), and intravascular large B-cell lymphoma. Mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma is potentially curable with good multi-year survival. In extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, survival tracks with the number of risk factors (B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH, regional node involvement), with 5-year survival ranging from 81% (zero risk factors) down to 7% (three to four factors). Chronic neutrophilic leukemia has a median survival of about 2 years, atypical CML around 10-25 months, and CMML survival ranges by Mayo Molecular Model risk from about 16 to 97 months. Histiocytic sarcoma has a poor prognosis with median survival measured in months to about 2 years.
pitfalls: Misclassifying nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma as classical Hodgkin's; the L&H 'popcorn' cell is a clonal B cell expressing CD45/CD79a/CD20/CD19/BCL2 and lacking CD30/CD15, behaving more like indolent B-cell NHL
Confusing B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia with leukemic mantle cell lymphoma, since both can express CD5 and t(11;14) and no reliable distinguishing criteria have emerged
Overlooking that a dry tap on marrow aspiration may signal hairy cell leukemia, myelofibrosis, metastatic carcinoma, CML, or acute leukemia rather than a technical failure
Mistaking lymphomatoid granulomatosis for extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, since both are angiodestructive and EBV-related
Attributing the presence of t(2;5) in a cutaneous CD30+ lesion to primary cutaneous disease; its presence should prompt evaluation for systemic anaplastic T-cell lymphoma
Failing to exclude reactive causes of neutrophilia, monocytosis, or eosinophilia before diagnosing CNL, CMML, or a primary eosinophilic disorder
Diagnosing systemic mastocytosis without accounting for hereditary alpha-tryptasemia when interpreting elevated serum tryptase
harrison.severityClassification: Several entities have formal staging/risk schemes. Myeloid neoplasms are classified by the ICC and WHO systems using blood counts, smear, marrow morphology, and cytogenetic/molecular tests. CMML is graded as CMML-1 (<10% marrow and <5% blood blasts) and CMML-2 (10-19% marrow or 5-19% blood blasts), with the Mayo Molecular Model assigning low to high risk by truncating ASXL1 mutation, absolute monocytes >10 x10^9/L, hemoglobin <10 g/dL, platelets <100 x10^9/L, and circulating immature myeloid cells. Systemic mastocytosis is subclassified into indolent, smoldering (requires two or more B findings), aggressive, SM with associated myeloid/hematologic neoplasm, and mast cell leukemia (>=20% mast cells in marrow aspirate); advanced SM is defined by an associated neoplasm or organopathy (C findings). Hypereosinophilia is defined as absolute eosinophil count >=1500 x10^9/L, with hypereosinophilic syndrome requiring eosinophil-mediated organ damage. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma nasal type uses a four-factor risk model (B symptoms, advanced stage, elevated LDH, regional node involvement).
management: Entity-specific therapy directed by precise histological and molecular classification, such as purine analogues (cladribine) or BRAF-directed therapy for hairy cell leukaemia

Rituximab-based immunochemotherapy for CD20-positive B-cell entities such as splenic marginal zone and mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma, with splenectomy for symptomatic splenic marginal zone disease
Tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy (imatinib) for eosinophilic neoplasms with PDGFRA or PDGFRB rearrangement, and KIT-directed therapy for advanced systemic mastocytosis
Treatment of underlying viral drivers, including antiretroviral therapy for HIV-associated HHV-8-driven primary effusion lymphoma
Alemtuzumab-based therapy for T-cell prolymphocytic leukaemia, with consideration of allogeneic stem cell transplantation
Supportive care with infection prophylaxis (especially given the monocytopenia of hairy cell leukaemia), transfusion support and management of cytopenias
Surveillance for organ involvement, including cardiac assessment for endomyocardial disease in hypereosinophilic syndrome
Referral to specialist haemato-oncology and consideration of clinical trials given the rarity of these entities
